title: Users and rights: who may do what
summary: Every file and every running program belongs to a user. Rights decide who reads, changes or runs what, and why nothing should run as root by habit.

text: Every file and every running program belongs to a user: a person, or a service.
- root is the administrator: no permission check stops it.
- Services get their own users, so a broken web server can't touch your files.
A group is a team of users. A file belongs to one user and one group.
- Rights are given three times: to the owner, to the group, to everyone else.
- Give rights to a team, not to each person: a newcomer joins the group and gets them all.

scheme: run     start it as a program
not sam, not in devs: others → nothing
text: Three rights: read, write, run. The system checks them each time a file is opened.
- "Permission denied" means this check said no, on the file or a folder on its path: the file is fine, your user lacks the right.
- The Linux path shows how to read and change them (ls -l, chmod).

scheme: ✘ everything as root     one mistake breaks all
✘ open to everyone       anyone can change it
✔ sudo for one command   root only when needed
✔ a user per service     a breach stays small
✔ rights for a group     not for everyone
text: Least privilege: give each user and program only the rights it needs.
- sudo runs one command as root, then you're yourself again.
- Opening a file to everyone to make an error go away trades a small problem for a security hole.
